content: Breast lumps are a common symptom experienced by women and can be detected either through self-examination or clinical breast examination. While many breast lumps are benign, they can also be the initial presentation of breast cancer, necessitating further clinical evaluation, imaging studies, and medical interventions. Benign breast diseases encompass a wide range of lesions originating from mammary epithelium or other breast tissues. Breast lumps may also be associated with vascular, inflammatory, or traumatic pathologies. Typically, breast lumps are palpable, nodular masses that may or may not exhibit specific characteristics. The initial step in evaluating a breast lump involves a clinical examination, followed by imaging studies such as mammography, ultrasound, or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) if the findings are suspicious. Management of breast lumps depends on the disease pattern, available resources, and specialist recommendations. Historically, breast diseases have been prevalent among women, but many were reluctant to discuss their symptoms publicly. In the 1970s, women with malignant breast lumps often underwent radical mastectomy without prior biopsies. Fine needle aspiration biopsy was introduced in the 1930s but became more widely used for breast lumps in the 1950s. Breast ultrasound also emerged in the 1950s, and mammography was developed in 1975 to aid in the early detection of breast cancer. Breast lumps can be classified based on epithelial hyperplasia into three subtypes: non-proliferative, proliferative disease, and proliferative disease without atypia. They can also be categorized histologically into lobular, ductal, or other origins. Breast development is influenced by hormones such as estrogen, progesterone, prolactin, and estradiol. The pathophysiology of breast lumps varies depending on their histological subtype. Hormonal events and genetic mutations are thought to contribute to the development of breast lumps. Gene mutations associated with breast cancer risk are classified into high-risk (e.g., BRCA1, BRCA2, TP53), moderate-risk (e.g., CHEK2, BRIP1, PALB2), and low-risk categories. The causes of breast lumps differ by gender and age. In women, they may result from cancer, inflammation, infection, hormonal imbalances, or trauma. In men, breast enlargement is often identified as gynecomastia. Breast lumps in children and adolescents are usually benign and related to pubertal changes. Differentiating breast lumps from other conditions, such as malignancies, cysts, inflammation, or non-inflammatory solid masses, is essential. Symptoms like nipple discharge and breast pain also require evaluation. Imaging findings and clinical breast examination results are used to distinguish different types of breast lumps. Benign breast diseases account for approximately 68% of all breast conditions, with a higher incidence in the left upper/outer quadrant of the breast. Fibrocystic changes are more common in women aged 40–44, while fibroadenomas are more frequent in women aged 15–35, with a higher prevalence among Black women. African-American women also tend to have worse prognoses and higher mortality rates compared to European-American women. Risk factors for breast lumps include age (with increasing cancer risk as women age), a history of breast disease or biopsy, a family history of breast cancer in first-degree relatives, genetic mutations (e.g., BRCA1, BRCA2), hormonal factors (e.g., age at menarche, first pregnancy, menopause, breastfeeding, parity), exogenous hormone use (e.g., contraceptive pills, hormone replacement therapy), and lifestyle factors (e.g., alcohol consumption, inactivity, obesity, prior radiation exposure). Screening for breast lumps is recommended through breast examination, ultrasound, mammography, and MRI. If benign breast lumps are confirmed through clinical and cytological evaluation, they do not typically become malignant, and 68% resolve over time, often within two years. However, some lumps initially thought to be benign may later be found to be malignant based on cytological results. In women under 35, benign lumps may resolve without excision. Mammography is the gold standard for diagnosing breast lumps in women over 40, while ultrasound is preferred for women under 40. MRI is used selectively when other imaging modalities yield inconclusive results. Imaging findings are often reported using the Breast Imaging Reporting and Data System (BI-RADS), which classifies findings into seven categories. Biopsy techniques include core-needle biopsy, open surgical biopsy, and fine needle aspiration biopsy. Core-needle biopsy can be guided by ultrasound, stereotactic imaging, MRI, or performed freehand. It has high sensitivity and specificity. Surgeons may use the triple test score, which includes clinical breast examination, fine needle aspiration, and mammography, or a modified version with core-needle biopsy and ultrasound, to assess palpable breast lumps. There is no specific medical therapy for breast lumps, but certain medications may be used prophylactically to reduce the risk of transformation into breast carcinoma. Surgical management depends on the type of mass identified through core-needle biopsy. Conditions such as atypical ductal hyperplasia, atypical lobular hyperplasia, lobular neoplasia, lobular carcinoma in situ, and flat epithelial atypia, among others, may require surgical consultation and excision. Other breast lumps may be managed with observation and follow-up. The decision for excisional biopsy is made collaboratively by pathologists, radiologists, and surgeons. There are no established measures for the primary prevention of breast lumps. Secondary prevention focuses on modifiable risk factors and protective measures to reduce breast cancer rates. These include controlling alcohol consumption, maintaining a healthy weight, engaging in physical activity, following a healthy diet, breastfeeding, prophylactic bilateral oophorectomy for BRCA1 and BRCA2 carriers, avoiding hormone replacement therapy, and using tamoxifen for high-risk women over 35. Surveillance and follow-up through physical examination and mammography are essential to reduce breast cancer recurrence.
